A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LiMVAM research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including relocated algorithms and renumbered results.

before.justification: v3 reports original synthetic experiments, Cam-CAN MEG analyses, fMRI causal graphs, and supplementary robustness results in Section 6 and Appendix H.

after.justification: v4 retains those original empirical results and adds a baseline comparison, diagnostic validation, and further assumption-violation experiments in Appendix H.

M1.justification: The causal estimators remain essentially unchanged, but H.1.4 adds an auxiliary post-estimation assumption diagnostic based on correlations and regression residuals. The full pseudocode also replaces mean subtraction with standardization, aligning it with standardized-variable assumptions already present in v3.

E1.justification: The synthetic causal-discovery task and both neuroimaging datasets are retained. New synthetic scenarios cover absent or vanishing cross-view correlations, varying mechanism changes, and mixtures of views sharing an ordering with independently ordered views.

E2.justification: The original six-method comparisons are retained. v4 additionally evaluates Perry et al.'s MSS using its KCI variant against DirectLiMVAM in the correlated-view experiment of H.1.3 and Figure 8.

E3.justification: Added simulations specify new controlled sweeps, including 0–6 mechanism changes and 0–20 views with different orderings, using 500- or 1000-sample configurations. The retained sparsity experiment's description corrects the eligible entries from 30 to 15; its unchanged plot does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: H.1.3–H.1.6 substantially expand analysis of the methods' assumptions: mechanism-change sensitivity, validation of the new diagnostic, vanishing correlations, and violations of shared ordering. Existing dimensionality, ICA noise-diversity, sparsity, and MEG stability analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The new MSS comparison specifies 30 random seeds, while the diagnostic, correlation-strength, and ordering-mismatch studies specify 100 seeds. Figure 9 displays the diagnostic's across-run distribution. Existing repetition counts and quartile reporting remain unchanged; increased replication of retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Figures 8–11 add results comparing MSS, validating the diagnostic, showing decreasing error with stronger correlations, and revealing severe degradation under ordering mismatch. Original plotted results are retained, including MEG stability correlations of 0.67 and 0.27. Section 6.3 also corrects LOCC-to-LACC from a direct edge to a path.

T1.justification: v4 Theorem 4 replaces v3 Theorem 2's complete pooled edge-support requirement for ordering identifiability with the weaker directed-path total-order condition, supported by a revised matrix-power proof in F.2. Appendix B.4 also corrects (I - B)^2 to I - B^2 in the residual and covariance derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain their scientific scope: LiMVAM, three algorithm adaptations, consistency and identifiability using second-order statistics without requiring non-Gaussianity, and neuroimaging validation. The rewritten conclusion restates claims already present in v3.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands applicability boundaries through the paired-view versus multi-domain distinction and stimulus-locked versus resting-state discussion. It interprets the new ordering-mismatch failures, qualifies their unusually severe perturbations, and explicitly discusses the diagnostic score's heuristic construction and limitations.

D1.justification: Section 6 adds an explicit LiMVAM repository link and identifies Python as the implementation language. New passages document the MSS implementation choice and diagnostic construction, although the latter's exact aggregation remains unspecified. Existing neuroimaging preprocessing, hardware/runtime information, and fMRI access instructions are retained.

R1.justification: Section 7 and new Appendix I substantially reposition the work against multi-domain and multi-environment approaches, including Ghassami, Adams, Peters, and Perry. The introduction also expands nonlinear and optimization-based context, while discussion of Shimizu changes from assuming independent views to ignoring their dependencies.

P1.justification: The exposition is substantially reorganized: Section 4 introduces the bivariate assumption before the criteria, presents existing consistency results as propositions, and incorporates the full algorithm from the appendix. The introduction, model explanation, discussion, and conclusion are revised, with an extended framework-comparison appendix added.

P2.justification: v4 adds explanatory diagrams for the model, algorithm, and bivariate assumption, plus four experimental figures with new comparison and diagnostic displays. It moves the full algorithm into the main text and rearranges existing figures. Original graphical results are retained rather than replaced.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important gap by directly testing the SOS methods' correlation and shared-ordering requirements, exposing failures and clarifying applicability. The corrected likelihood derivation and weaker connectivity requirement with a revised proof also strengthen the theoretical account. These substantial gains outweigh the diagnostic's unspecified aggregation and Figure 8's textual claim of perfect recovery despite small dips in the plotted performance.
